name: Red clover extract
summary: Red clover is a plant whose flowers contain isoflavones, plant compounds that act weakly like estrogen. Extracts are sold mainly for menopause symptoms.
commonUses: May reduce hot flushes (sudden waves of heat) in women around and after menopause.
May ease other menopause symptoms, such as vaginal dryness.
May support the effects of low estrogen, the main female sex hormone, in women after menopause.
May help bone density after menopause.
May improve skin fullness, wrinkles and hydration.
roles: Red clover isoflavones bind weakly to estrogen receptors, but no essential role in the body is known. The evidence for easing hot flushes is mixed and small.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Not eaten as a food; used as a leaf and flower extract

forms.name: Standardised flower extract
forms.note: The form used in most trials, labelled by isoflavone content.

forms.name: Tablets or capsules with other herbs
forms.note: Often combined with soy, black cohosh or others; harder to judge what worked.

forms.name: Herbal tea or dried herb
forms.note: Isoflavone content is unknown and varies.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level has been set for isoflavones. EFSA assessed isolated isoflavone food supplements for women around and after menopause in 2015. In the studies it reviewed, up to 150 mg a day for up to 30 months did not change the breast, thyroid hormone levels or the lining of the uterus. It could not set a safe intake level, and said long-term high intake is not without risk for this group, because breast cancer risk rises after menopause. These are population findings, not a personal limit.

sources.title: Risk assessment for peri- and post-menopausal women taking food supplements containing isolated isoflavones

interactions.with: Hormone therapy, tamoxifen and other hormone-related medicines
interactions.note: Red clover isoflavones act weakly like estrogen, so it is not known how they interact. A doctor or pharmacist should be told.
Red clover is traditionally said to affect clotting. Good human data are lacking, so people on blood thinners should check with their doctor before use.

cautions: People with a history of breast, ovarian or uterine cancer, or other hormone-sensitive conditions, should talk to their doctor before using isoflavone supplements. Reviews found no clear harm in observational data, but long-term supplement trials in these groups are limited.
Not for use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and not for children, because safety has not been shown.
Hot flushes, bleeding after menopause, or bone loss need a doctor's assessment, not self-treatment with a supplement.

origin: Red clover (Trifolium pratense) is a meadow plant used as animal feed and in traditional herbal medicine. Its flowers contain isoflavones, plant compounds with a shape similar to estrogen. The main ones are biochanin A and formononetin, which the body converts to genistein and daidzein. They can bind weakly to estrogen receptors, which is why they are called phytoestrogens (plant estrogens). Whether this has a useful effect in the body is the open question.

Supplements are extracts of the flowers or leaves, standardised to an isoflavone content. Soy isoflavones are a different mix: red clover is richer in biochanin A and formononetin, soy in genistein and daidzein. Red clover is not a common food, so most people only meet it in supplements or herbal teas.
dosage: There is no reference intake for red clover or for isoflavones. EFSA assessed isolated isoflavone food supplements for women around and after menopause in 2015. In the studies it reviewed, up to 150 mg a day for up to 30 months did not change the breast, thyroid hormone levels or the lining of the uterus. It could not set a safe intake level, and said long-term high intake is not without risk for this group, because breast cancer risk rises after menopause. These are population findings, not a personal limit.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 40 to 80 mg of isoflavones a day. A 2021 meta-analysis found the clearest effect on hot flushes at 80 mg a day or more, over 12 weeks. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When reading a label, check whether the number is the total isoflavones or the weight of the whole extract. An extract of 500 mg may hold only 40 mg of isoflavones. Also check which isoflavones are listed, because red clover and soy products are not the same mix. Several products can add up.
